title: From Agency Recruiters to In-House Hiring for Startups (September 2026)
summary: September 2026 guide for startups ready to leave agency recruiters behind and build a cost-effective in-house recruiting process.
body_markdown:
Every[agency placement](https://www.dover.com/) comes with a percentage fee attached, and as hiring volume grows, those fees start to look less like a cost of doing business and more like a budget line worth owning directly. Founders typically reach a fork: keep routing searches through agencies and pay per placement, or build an internal recruiting process that compounds over time. This guide covers how to make that move in practice, from auditing your current pipeline to standing up the tools and support that keep hiring momentum intact during the transition.


**TLDR:**


-


Agency contingency fees typically run 15-30% of first-year salary, making in-house hiring more cost-effective as hiring scales.


-


Structured recruiting support, whether fractional or in-house, can cut time to hire by nearly 30% vs. hiring managers running searches alone (Ashby 2026 Startup Hiring Trends).


-


A successful agency-to-in-house transition requires auditing your pipeline, securing a knowledge transfer, and overlapping processes briefly to avoid cold starts.


-


Fractional recruiters offer on-demand expertise billed for time worked, averaging about $4,800 per hire, without the overhead of a full-time hire.


-


Some tools pair free ATS software with on-demand recruiting support, giving seed-stage teams a repeatable hiring process without enterprise-level cost.


## The 2026 Recruiting Market: Why the Shift Is Accelerating


A few developments in 2026 have made the case for in-house recruiting more concrete. Ashby’s[2026 Startup Hiring Trends report](https://www.ashbyhq.com/talent-trends-report/reports/startup-hiring) found that over half of startup talent teams are now using AI across multiple hiring workflows, meaning the tooling gap between a scrappy internal process and an agency’s operations has narrowed considerably. At the same time, agency fee structures haven’t budged: contingency placements still typically land between 15% and 30% of first-year salary, which on a $120K engineering hire translates to $18,000 to $36,000 per placement.


The data on speed is also worth noting. For startups under 25 employees, Ashby found that involving a recruiter early (whether fractional or in-house) cut time to hire by nearly 30% compared to hiring managers running searches alone. The implication isn’t that you need an agency; it’s that structured recruiting support, built into your own process, moves faster than ad hoc outreach while costing a fraction of contingency fees.


Remote roles are drawing 42% more inbound applications than in-office equivalents, which adds its own filtering challenge.[2025 job application volume data](https://blog.hiringthing.com/2025-job-application-statistics-updated-data-you-need-to-know) shows many postings now receive 100 or more applications, making an ATS and a repeatable screening process less optional and more foundational, even for a team making only a handful of hires a year.


## Why Build an In-House Recruiting Process Early


Bringing hiring in-house treats recruitment as a core workflow for your startup. It’s an investment, but the benefits are substantial:


-


Save money by eliminating agency fees


-


Build deeper candidate relationships and institutional knowledge that agencies don’t retain


-


Create your own talent database for future needs


-


Get data to make smarter hiring decisions


-


Quickly adjust recruiting as your startup grows


The cost difference adds up quickly. At 10 hires a year with an average first-year salary of $100K, a 20% contingency fee runs $200,000 in agency costs alone.[SHRM’s 2025 cost-per-hire benchmarks](https://www.shrm.org/about/press-room/shrm-releases-2025-benchmarking-reports--how-does-your-organizat) put the average in-house cost per non-executive hire at $5,475, well below what contingency fees add per placement. An in-house setup (even one that includes a fractional recruiter at hourly rates and an ATS) typically runs well under half of what agency fees would cost, and those costs don’t scale linearly with every new hire you make.

With an internal recruiting engine, you’re building a strategic capability that compounds over time, instead of paying per transaction. This approach sets you up to scale your team efficiently as you grow.


Dover’s model is built for exactly this stage. The free ATS gives seed-stage and early Series A teams pipeline infrastructure from day one, including job postings, candidate tracking, and a careers page, without a monthly cost or setup overhead. Many teams start there to build process and track every candidate in one place, then add a fractional recruiter from Dover’s marketplace when a role is stalling or requires active outreach the team doesn’t have bandwidth for. The result is a recruiting setup that grows with the company instead of resetting at each funding stage.


## Preparing for a Smooth Transition


Switching from agencies requires careful planning to avoid disrupting candidate pipelines and searches. Here are key preparation steps:


1.


**Audit current recruiting pipeline:** List all open roles, active candidates, statuses, and notes.


2.


**Communicate internally:** Align your team on the new in-house process.


3.


**Coordinate knowledge transfer:** Collect candidate info, resumes, notes, and insights from current agencies.


4.


**Time the transition:** Briefly overlap old and new processes to prevent cold starts on roles.


5.


**Document everything:** Record the transition plan, timelines, and key agency insights.


6.


**Check contracts:** Review notice periods, fees, terms around candidate ownership and submissions.


7.


**Identify recruiting owner(s):** Decide who will own and drive the new in-house process (founder, new hire, etc.).


Thorough preparation prevents candidates from slipping through the cracks during the handover from agencies.


## Setting Up Your Recruiting Infrastructure


To bring recruiting in-house, you need the right infrastructure and tech stack, starting with an Applicant Tracking System (ATS), which is software that centralizes all hiring activities in one place. Options like our[free ATS](https://www.dover.com/ats) take minutes to set up for job posting, candidate tracking, and a careers site.


**Scheduling and coordination:** Use calendar integrations to automate interview scheduling, reminders, and team coordination. Tools like Dover integrate with Slack for easy communication.


**Using AI and smart tools:** Modern ATS can score resumes to surface top candidates, reducing manual screening time.


**Multi-channel approach:** Collect candidates across job boards, referrals, LinkedIn, and other sources, tracking their origin in the ATS.


**Employee referral programs:** Implement a simple way for your team to submit referrals, which feed directly into your ATS pipeline.


**Process and training:** Define clear hiring workflows and train your team on using the new tools and providing feedback.


With smart recruiting software, teams can process high hiring volumes even with limited bandwidth and resources. Tracking the right[recruiting metrics for startups](https://www.dover.com/blog/recruiting-metrics-for-startups) helps you measure whether your process is actually working. When those metrics show that sourcing is the bottleneck, with open roles not generating enough qualified pipeline, that’s the clearest signal that pairing a fractional recruiter with your ATS makes more sense than spending more time on job board tweaks. The ATS tells you where the process breaks; the recruiter fixes the specific stage that software can’t.


## Bridging the Gap with Fractional Recruiters


Fractional recruiters provide professional hiring help on a flexible, hourly basis, bridging the gap between agencies and full-time hires.


An ATS handles inbound volume, pipeline tracking, and coordination. It is the working layer you need regardless of what else you add. When a role is senior, specialized, or sitting open longer than expected, that’s the decision point where human sourcing capacity starts to matter. A fractional recruiter works within that same ATS to drive outreach on searches self-serve tools alone can’t close.


**What is a fractional recruiter?** An experienced recruitment pro you hire for set hours/projects, not a salaried employee. These professionals bring the same depth as[HR specialists in full-time roles](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/business-and-financial/human-resources-specialists.htm) , but on a flexible engagement model that fits startup hiring cycles instead of requiring a permanent headcount addition.


**Benefits of fractional recruiting:**


-


Expertise without the overhead of a full time hire


-


Cost transparency: you pay for time worked, and recruiters set their own rates


-


Simple team integration using your tools like an ATS


-


On-demand flexibility to scale their hours


-


High touch, quality focus over volume


-


Dedicated attention on *your* specific roles and needs


**Finding fractional recruiters:** Use a service like Dover’s[expert recruiter marketplace](https://www.dover.com/recruiters) . Or find someone via your network with relevant experience.


**When to use fractional:** During transition periods to prevent hiring lulls, for short-term hiring sprints, executive searches, or whenever hiring needs fluctuate.


Fractional recruiters provide speed, flexibility, and expertise which is exactly what startups need for efficient hiring without breaking the bank.


## Hiring Tools Most YC Startups Actually Use


When early-stage YC-backed teams set up their first in-house recruiting stack, a few tools come up consistently. The pattern reflects where different tools sit in the startup growth curve and what tradeoffs matter most at seed versus Series A and beyond.


**Ashby** has become the most talked-about ATS among growth-stage YC companies. It combines ATS, CRM, scheduling, and analytics in one system, and its reporting depth is genuinely distinctive: teams can track pipeline velocity and bottleneck stages without exporting to a spreadsheet. The tradeoff is setup overhead and pricing: Foundations starts around $400/month, with custom quotes for teams beyond 100 employees. It fits best when a dedicated recruiter is already in place and will actually use the analytics layer.


**Greenhouse** tends to show up at later-stage YC companies (Series B and beyond) with mature HR infrastructure already in place. Its integration library is broad (500+ connectors), and the workflow controls appeal to teams that need process consistency across multiple hiring managers. For most pre-Series A teams, it’s more infrastructure than the moment calls for.


**Lever** is a strong fit when the team is running both active pipelines and longer-term talent nurturing simultaneously, since it combines ATS and CRM in one system, which reduces tool sprawl for teams doing proactive sourcing alongside inbound hiring.


**Wellfound** (formerly AngelList Talent) serves a different function: it’s primarily a job board and candidate marketplace where YC startups post roles to reach candidates who are drawn to startup environments, not a full ATS. Many teams use it alongside their primary ATS for sourcing. YC’s own[Work at a Startup](https://www.workatastartup.com/) platform also aggregates open roles across the YC portfolio and is worth listing on regardless of which ATS you use.


For seed-stage teams that haven’t yet hired their first recruiter, lighter-weight options (including Dover’s[free ATS](https://www.dover.com/ats) ) can handle the job posting, candidate tracking, and basic pipeline management without the setup overhead or monthly cost of enterprise tools. The right ATS for your stage is the one you’ll actually use consistently, not the one with the longest feature list. The ATS is the foundation; a fractional recruiter is what you add on top when a search needs more active sourcing than your team has bandwidth for.

That is the structural difference between a fractional model and a contingency agency, and it is what makes the transition from agency-led to in-house hiring durable over time.


## FAQs


### What’s the real cost difference between agency contingency fees and fractional recruiting for startups?


Agency contingency fees typically run 15 to 30% of first-year salary, which translates to $18,000 to $36,000 on a $120,000 engineering hire. Fractional recruiters working through a service like Dover’s marketplace bill for time worked, and hires average about $4,800 all-in, with no placement fee tied to salary.


### Should I transition from agency recruiting to in-house before or after my first ATS is set up?


Set up the ATS first, then begin the transition. Migrating active candidate pipelines from your agency into the ATS before cutting off the engagement prevents candidates from slipping through the handover, and gives your team a working system to coordinate interviews from day one of running searches internally.


### Ashby vs. Dover free ATS for a seed-stage startup without a dedicated recruiter?


Ashby is a strong fit once a dedicated recruiter is already in place to get value from its analytics depth, but its Foundations plan starts around $400/month and carries meaningful setup overhead. Dover’s free ATS requires no monthly cost and takes under five minutes to set up, making it a better starting point for founder-led hiring before dedicated recruiting headcount is in place.


## Final Thoughts on Moving Hiring In-House


Switching from[agency recruiting](https://www.dover.com/) to an in-house process is a structural decision as much as a financial one. The cost savings are real and compound with each hire, but the more durable benefit is owning your pipeline data, your candidate relationships, and your sourcing knowledge instead of starting cold each time. When that shift makes sense depends on hiring volume, bandwidth, and how much of your recruiting currently lives inside someone else’s system. Dover is one place to start: a free ATS handles pipeline tracking and job distribution from day one, and fractional recruiters from Dover’s marketplace can step in when a role needs active sourcing that self-serve tools alone can’t close. Some teams make the move at seed stage; others wait until agency costs become impossible to ignore. Either way, the infrastructure to support it doesn’t have to be complicated or expensive to put in place.
